MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents

MCPHallu is a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution and memory. It contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers, with each task built around a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse or Context Forgetting, enabling subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success. Fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors were evaluated over 5,012 trajectories, with current MCP agents remaining vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments at an average score of 0.642 on a 0-1 scale, with failures concentrated on reasoning-side subtypes.
Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs

A preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks compares free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs in which the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger decision. With Qwen3-8B over 1,440 trajectories and five threats, signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4 percent to 9.0 percent, a 60.4 point improvement with 95 percent CI [51.4, 69.4], with no net loss of conformant commits versus structured handoffs. An unsigned manifest committed violations in 79 percent of mutated runs, the signed one in none, and on identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7 percent of violating decisions versus 59.0 percent for an LLM checker, with 7 percent versus 50 percent false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits, showing residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing.
Authorization Propagation in Agent2Agent Systems: An Experimental Security Evaluation of Multi-Hop Delegation

Delegated Agent2Agent workflows create a security problem when the agent sending a request differs from the principal the authority originated from. The paper evaluates a layered downstream-verification design in a synthetic four-party healthcare reimbursement workflow, separating current-caller context, transitive authorization evidence, per-hop Ed25519 request authentication and independent replay state for requests and authorization artifacts. Of 15 adversarial conditions, 14 are rejected, with an isolated delegation-path test exposing the absence of semantic authority attenuation. A separate authorized-intermediary experiment shows that a holder of the shared authorization-evidence HMAC key can modify the represented authority and generate valid evidence. In the fixed-depth local benchmark the full configuration has a median security-processing latency of 5.11 ms and a 3.87 kB serialized payload, leading the authors to call for origin-verifiable delegation and semantic attenuation for stronger A2A authorization propagation.
SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection

Tool-using agents act on email, files and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker text. SPILLWAY instead reads where an action goes from the tools typed returns, since an email sender or a payment account arrives in a typed field while injected instructions arrive as free text, turning this into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. A call is admitted when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call but never one whose target lies in the removed text.
Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks

Indirect prompt-injection benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task, but attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress, as when a buyer dispute evidence cites a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. The paper defines IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording, treating planted content as an attack when it attempts to influence a decision its source is not authorized to determine. The benchmark makes the boundary explicit across 90 validated cases in three tool-use environments, where the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision and every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task. Each case targets up to six parts of the agent decision making: objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, and beliefs about current state, and without a defense attacks on decision rules, available actions and state succeed.
Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies

Multi-agent LLM system performance depends not only on model capabilities but on information-sharing policies governing what each agent observes and at what level of detail, and the paper asks whether more transparency can paradoxically degrade efficiency. It introduces empirical information design, an experimental framework systematically comparing disclosure policies across economic markets populated by LLM agents while holding interaction rules and models fixed. Ten frontier LLMs are evaluated in multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining and double auctions, using ground-truth utilities to decouple identified opportunities from realized outcomes. Finer disclosure yields highly model-dependent results: in trade, revealing exact valuations rather than ordinal preference rankings reduces realized gains for GPT-6 Sol from 98 to 91 percent of maximum yet increases them for Claude Sonnet 5 from 72 to 86 percent, and in bargaining exact information leads Grok 4.7 to produce less balanced agreements.
Trilemma: How Agents choose between Honesty, Confidentiality, and Task Completion

Personal AI agents often act on underspecified instructions and draw on context such as user messages and calendar, which can contain private preferences that interfere with the task, with other people interests, or with confidentiality norms. Prior work studied deception under goal conflicts and leakage of private information largely as separate problems; this paper studies both together in a simulated company Slack workspace where four employees delegate sprint staffing to personal agents. Two agents learn from private messages that their employee avoids a particular colleague, and because the other agents request justifications for task preferences while the only true justification is confidential, the agents cannot simultaneously remain honest, preserve confidentiality and complete the staffing. Across seven open-weight models plus Claude and GPT models, of the 135 of 140 open-weight agents that pursue the avoidance preference, 107 either make false claims about task fit or logistics or cite a true consideration as if it were their actual reason.
More Agents, More Reliable? System-Level Reliability of Multi-Agent LLMs under Operational-Profile Uncertainty

Teams increasingly build software from cooperating LLM agents while often assuming more agents mean more reliability, but the usual evidence, average benchmark accuracy, ignores the input mix a deployed system meets and the rule merging agent answers. Building on HIP-LLM, a hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of single LLMs, the paper proposes a framework combining it with a Bayesian network of the system failure logic for multi-agent systems. Agent failure-probability intervals propagate through the network, where the combining rule can itself fail, into a reliability envelope showing which evidence limits it. In a pipeline extracting regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest but did not clearly exceed the best, and a voter failing on 5 percent of demands would largely erase its advantage over the middle model, leading to the conclusion that more agents yield a more defensible reliability claim rather than automatically a more reliable system.
Take It From Here: Evaluating Coding Agents On Project Takeover

Coding agents increasingly collaborate on long-term projects and when taking over a project they must recover currently applicable requirements from interaction history and update them in response to new requests, but most coding benchmarks lack long interaction histories and some evaluations that consider history still do not cover the full process from requirement reconstruction to project delivery. The evaluation provides agents with the interaction history, current request and pre-request project environment, asks them to make the requested changes and assesses takeover performance through delivery tests. Across six model-harness configurations and 37 targets eligible for executable validation, the mean complete-delivery rate under Full History is only 4.95 percent, and requirement atoms are then used to diagnose a larger set of takeover targets covering relevant information identification, pre-request state reconstruction and current request processing.
The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks

The paper argues frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks, with GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolving 37.3 percent of Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8 percent, because tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, called the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. Agent-native primitives are reusable units equipping a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO is a harness engineering framework that builds each task harness from a library of such primitives, composing the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifying results against environment evidence, revising primitives a failure implicates and admitting new or improved primitives after validation.
Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations

After a runtime or API migration an LLM-repaired procedure can run cleanly yet return wrong results, and a release check on typical test inputs ships it. A preregistered study of 73 tasks covering 60 documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite executes every candidate on the real runtimes against withheld contracts. Over the complete repair space the all-assertions gate on typical inputs released 0.410 of wrong repairs, one edge input written from the release note cut this to 0.065 and to 0.061 on 15 unseen clusters, and three inputs from a blind GPT-5.6-luna writer that never saw the program reached 0.070. Two further frozen stages enlarged the menu to 1,491 fragments and added 233 hard distractors matching legacy output on typical inputs, yet 0.168 and 0.153 of the hard wrong programs still passed, while two local-model writers failed their preregistered tests.
ZeroRAG: Adaptive Semantic Peer Routing for Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation

RAG systems today collect, index and serve documents from centralized stores, but in practice documents are owned by organizations, devices and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody to a central party because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority or rely on a global data structure requiring continuous network-wide coordination such as DHTs. ZeroRAG is a decentralized routing layer performing semantic query routing across an overlay of peers without global data structures or centralized orchestration, keeping documents with their owning peers, each peer holding only lightweight local state including a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries, and steering each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically better peers.
Enhancing Local and Global Structure in Compressed AI Agent Memory

AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale, and a compression is accepted when each item nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. The work evaluates both ends with two label-free fidelities, a local fidelity L at 10 neighbors and a global fidelity G at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach L of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme, while PCA with 8-bit codes at L of 0.77 moves 1.7 percent. The authors prove that across the G band, 1-nu_k is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and derive a locality-aware quantization whose objective comes from that bound.
CORE: Coarse-to-Fine Search with Context Management for Deep Research

Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search and rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context, creating a trade-off because search works best over long passages which give enough context for reliable semantic matching, but returned evidence should be short because every observation stays in the agent context for the rest of the trajectory. CORE is a training-free harness combining coarse-to-fine search with context management, retrieving passages with a dense retriever and reusing token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage, while context management lets the agent expand context around already retrieved sources and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses it achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks on corpora up to 553M documents.
Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency

Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent, a design choice affecting how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives and what must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. The paper compares skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and a persistent retrieval subagent that maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent, with the main agent able to request corrections from the same subagent. Across five multi-turn settings the persistent approach uses 43.3 percent fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0 percent lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval while reducing average response time by 9.1 percent, though versus non-persistent retrieval it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question at 65.1 percent more tokens.

In 2003 Clark and colleagues proposed the Knowledge Plane, a layer of intelligent agents that share rich information about network state in order to collaboratively manage the Internet across administrative boundaries, but the technology of the day lacked the two capabilities it demanded most, reasoning and unstructured communication, so automated network management has remained largely confined to single domains while interdomain problems are still resolved by human operators on the phone. The paper argues that agentic large language models can finally unlock the potential of the Knowledge Plane, but that doing so requires solving new research problems arising particularly in this decentralized, multi-agent, coopetitive setting that have received limited attention in the literature.
ChemE-as-Code: An Open-Source Platform for Agentic AI in Chemical Engineering

ChemE-as-Code provides an open-source environment in which LLM-based agents can carry out chemical engineering work and engineers can check it, with calculation tools ranging from catalysis through process simulation to plant layout, HAZOP and life cycle assessment, and skills telling a general-purpose agent how to use them. Engineering files are linked, machine-readable and versioned in Git, calculations run outside the LLM, each value records its origin, and automated checks report inconsistencies and out-of-date results by file and line. In an illustrative ammonia case, agents developed a written task into a preliminary basic-engineering package including simulation files, P&IDs, layout, HAZOP, datasheets and relief for USD 224 of API cost, and planted faults show the checks find what their rules cover and miss the rest, so they guide human review rather than replace it. No independent engineer has reviewed the design.
tok: a textual concrete syntax of BPMN and DMN for humans and AI agents

tok is a plain-text notation for BPMN 2.0.2 process models and DMN 1.5 decisions, where one engine checks a tok document against both standards, compiles it to XML with an automatic diagram, and serves language-model applications through the Model Context Protocol. The paper classifies the notation as an alternative concrete syntax of the BPMN and DMN metamodels: a tok model takes 2.2 times fewer tokens than the smallest BPMN XML of 893 files exported by 37 tools and 7.7 times fewer than the files as exported, the checker signals 98.2 percent of 1,411 injected faults against 85.8 percent for XML Schema with bpmnlint, and four language models new to tok write valid tok from a one-page reference for 85.7 to 100 percent of 87 process descriptions from two datasets.
Create Your Own Work Stack: Deploying Self-hosted AI and Tooling in a Tech Startup

Self-hosting AI is often presented as a way to reduce inference costs and increase control, but deployment introduces its own costs. The paper reports experience deploying a hybrid AI stack at Grayhat Developers, a small software company with an AI-intensive development workflow, motivated to counter growing commercial AI cost, with Claude and Codex incurring approximately $325 per month and more than 25.93 billion recorded tokens. Local open-source models proved insufficient in performance and inference speed, so a hybrid approach was adopted in which commercial agents remained responsible for complex tasks while local models handled lower-complexity tasks, organizational information retrieval and synchronization with self-hosted tools including Outline, Plane and ERPNext, with an estimated 30 to 40 percent of the commercial AI workload associated with context transfer, documentation synchronization and task management, roughly 90 percent of which could be moved.
Agent-R^2: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis

Current agents still struggle to finish realistic productivity tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements, and a key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data reflecting real work intent, authentic file environments and deliverable-level evaluation. Agent-R^2 is a real-source data synthesis framework that grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence and authentic web-sourced files instead of manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files. From 10k web-corpus candidates it distills 4k task instances pairing real multi-format attachments with fine-grained deliverable-level rubrics, used to train a 4B agent via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement.
SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods, but the process is slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought per round and must repeat this many times to maintain population diversity. SwarmEvolve has hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text and share information by passing KV caches, with each swarm studying the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring distances between agents hidden state vectors, and crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing it gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach best scores other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes.
Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks

Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important, yet even benchmarks carefully validated at release become stale as models discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject and changes to evaluation infrastructure invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. The paper calls the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt and introduces a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks combining community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks and human-gated repairs. Applied to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release, the audit identifies issues in roughly 30 percent of the benchmark and the repairs released as Terminal-Bench 2.1 change evaluation results, with accuracy increasing by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions moving by up to three ranks.
Who Can Evaluate AI Independently? A Framework for Analysing Evaluation Infrastructure

AI evaluation is increasingly central to AI safety and governance, yet taking part in an evaluation does not by itself confer authority over its design, its execution or the resources it depends on. The paper examines how infrastructure arrangements distribute that authority and therefore shape who can evaluate AI systems independently, drawing on Science and Technology Studies, political economy and applied evaluation standards to introduce PAAI, a framework covering power, access, adequacy and independence. It is applied to twelve African AI evaluation projects from 2022 to 2025 and to the documented roles of all ten member institutes in the three published joint testing exercises of the international network of AI Safety Institutes, identifying three recurring configurations: extractive collaboration, dependent innovation and constrained independence, with African actors often contributing data, language expertise and task design while external institutions retain authority over infrastructure and evaluation frameworks.
The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance

Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context, meaning irrelevant statements from unrelated domains or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query, and such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using and long-context deployments. The paper traces the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources, but preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. The interference is then localized to a sparse set of attention heads called intrusion heads, whose prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, with the same heads transferring across tasks and distractor types and largely weight-disjoint from heads integrating relevant content.
AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL

Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. AttnSR is a step-level reward augmentation method deriving reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts, tracing backward through the policy model attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response, with the terminal step measured relative to a running baseline determining whether these rewards reinforce or penalize the selected steps. In a controlled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study it consistently outperforms the PPO baseline across all evaluated checkpoints on ALFWorld, raising final held-out success from 91.2 to 97.1 percent, and improves ScienceWorld at every checkpoint while cutting environment interactions by 29.9 percent.
SMART: State-based Multi Agent Reasoning Traces for Verification-oriented Problem-Solving

Complex problems with limited context, such as claims, require a means to obtain additional knowledge necessary for solution reasoning. SMART is a multi-agent framework that obtains knowledge by capturing the implicit state of participating entities in a problem context, curating state knowledge as diverse, complementary and solution-salient premises using a variety of LLMs and a structured role-based prompt strategy. Using knowledge from real-world verified curated premises, knowledge-guided solution reasoning improves validation performance up to 20 percent on complex scientific claims spanning three datasets, and the paper shows grounding premises in real-world knowledge is necessary and improves performance up to 5 percent.
The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record

Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models, orchestration harnesses and systems of record, but finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period, so the business question of what an order, claim or case cost in AI cannot be answered from billing data because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps FOCUS specification gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain. The paper formalizes this grain mismatch, derives seven requirements and proposes the Two-Ledger Model, a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry, with a layered correlation spine using trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation and probabilistic matching to assign each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence.
Octopus: One Brain, Many Branches for Latent-KV Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Multi-agent LLM systems explore in parallel by spawning sub-agents with isolated context windows, while existing multi-agent frameworks duplicate prefix KV caches across branches, exchange findings by re-prefilling text summaries, and flatten or drop cross-branch dependencies during reinforcement learning. Octopus is a single-model multi-agent RL framework in which all threads share one backbone and coordinate over a GPU-resident directed acyclic graph of KV states through five primitives, fork, read_thread, wait_threads, rewind and commit. It combines Zero-Copy Radix Forking spawning branches as O(1) cursor views over shared physical KV pages, Attention-Only KV Mounting mounting a sibling thread terminal KV blocks directly into full-attention layers while bypassing linear-recurrent states to cut off-task hijacking by 21 times from 57.9 to 2.7 percent while retaining 92.2 percent of full-text mutual information at zero extra KV allocation, and a Packed DAG-GRPO trainer.
SCALE: Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents

Latent communication lets agents collaborate efficiently by directly exchanging intermediate model representations rather than raw sensor data or text messages, but existing approaches are primarily designed for LLM agents and do not consider bandwidth constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines faced by cyber-physical agents. SCALE matches tokens across consecutive latent messages using similarity scores to identify reusable information and avoid redundant transmission, profiles the semantic gain and communication cost of transmitting different amounts of latent information, and employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which pending messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send subject to available bandwidth and task deadlines, evaluated across three cyber-physical benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions.
SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments

Multi-agent reinforcement learning is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment, and while policy inference can be batched on GPUs, the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions and builds observations inside each env.step, a path that can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. SEER is a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract, modelling each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events so that if direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, independent events can run in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs, implemented with a CAS-based dual-layer event queue.
Learning Multi-Agent Orchestration: Higher-Order Interactions in Policy Improvement

Learned orchestration has emerged as a promising paradigm for LLM-based multi-agent systems in which a central orchestrator selects agents and controls the information they receive, but existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming other decisions in the episode stay fixed, an assumption that fails where the contribution of each decision depends on preceding decisions. IAPO is an interaction-aware policy optimization framework that exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, proving interactions can account for half of the attainable gain, then optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying every update is an improvement, evaluated on long-input versions of GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval against fifteen published baselines.
Secure Formal Raising: Protecting the Development of AI through Executable Properties

Model raising revisits the Turing developmental view of machine intelligence, and Formal Raising has recently been proposed to complement that view with explicit behavioral properties. This paper extends that proposal to the security of the raising environment, modeling policy integrity, authorization and confidential data flow using four-valued evidence that preserves unknown and inconsistent assessments, proving six security invariants and showing they force admission to accept only confirmed evidence. A plain-C reference implementation satisfies the invariants in a bounded exhaustive exploration, which also exposes a confused-deputy gap for tool calls that a provenance requirement closes.
tau-bench-LILT: Evaluating Conversational Agents on Realistic Multilingual Tool-Use Tasks

Frontier evaluations of tool-using conversational agents are conducted almost exclusively in English, leaving a critical gap for organizations deploying agents in other languages and regions. tau-bench-LILT is a multilingual extension of tau3-bench covering German, Korean, Turkish and Farsi in the airline, retail, telecom and banking domains, natively localizing every layer with culturally appropriate customer database records, user-simulator prompts refined iteratively through contrastive annotation by native-language experts, and tasks updated according to the localized database. Evaluation across eight agent models shows the largest drops compared to English in the Korean and Farsi retail domains, by up to 61 points in pass at four.
Evaluating Token Probabilities as Confidence Estimators in Human Behavior Simulations

As LLMs are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, their operational validity is typically assessed through accuracy alone, implicitly treating human behavior as deterministic, while on noisy digital trace data performance depends not only on predicting the correct outcome but on calibration. The case study tests whether token probabilities of open-weight LLMs can serve as confidence estimates in a Next Like Prediction task on the Luxembourgish news platform RTL.lu, evaluating Ministral 3 at 3B and 8B and finding that with in-context learning only the models are overconfident and outperformed on accuracy and calibration by a simple statistical baseline, that scaling from 3B to 8B improves accuracy while degrading calibration, and that task-specific supervised fine-tuning reduces Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while improving accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758.
METR: Anthropic may have crossed its own AI acceleration warning threshold back in July

METR got eleven weeks of access to Anthropic internal research data and found that the rate at which Anthropic models improve has roughly doubled, with about 80 percent of that acceleration tracing back to AI being used in the company own research. Anthropic redacted the most important evidence, and whether AI is speeding up development of better AI is a key early warning signal in the safety debate, because a feedback loop could form where models improve their successors faster and faster and lead, per METR, to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities. Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy flags exactly this as a risk indicator: if the pace of AI progress doubles because of automated AI research that should trigger a warning level. From August 12 to October 29, 2026, a team of 2.5 full-time staffers received benchmark results from unreleased models, training metrics, employee surveys and internal analyses, plus roughly 15 interviews with Anthropic researchers, and METR took no money from Anthropic while working on Anthropic devices for security reasons. Since October 2025 Anthropic model test scores have climbed about 1.9 times faster than between March 2024 and October 2025 on the AECI composite metric, meaning Anthropic achieved in one year what previously took two, roughly comparable to the jump from Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5, with the rate rising from about 15 AECI points per year to 29 and three unreleased models trained between July and October 2026 included. Anthropic had recently committed to bringing external auditors in and announced a METR collaboration involving employee-like access in October.
Anthropic $1.5 trillion IPO hits resistance as investors balk at valuation

Anthropic IPO is in trouble as investors push back on the $1.5 trillion valuation and the tech market sells off, according to Reuters, with potential backers doubting the planned roadshow can kick off next week as scheduled. As recently as September the company was eyeing a valuation of up to $2 trillion, and now some investors think even $1.5 trillion is too rich, one reportedly floating a valuation of just $1 trillion. Investors want a steeper discount because Anthropic is still losing money and burning through cash to scale AI infrastructure, and they are waiting on October revenue numbers that are missing from the updated S-1 filing. The midterm elections made things worse as ballot initiatives targeting data center expansion passed in several states, triggering the sharpest tech selloff in a year, and the Wall Street Journal also reports IPO investors are skeptical. If AI stocks stay under pressure Anthropic could delay the offering, which some estimates peg at up to $100 billion in size, and a delay could further shake confidence in the broader AI sector.
Perplexity launches Teammates, an always-on AI agent that works around the clock

Perplexity now has its own AI agent that runs around the clock and handles work tasks on its own. While Perplexity Computer executes one-off assignments, the new Teammates stay active and work through ongoing projects independently, with each Teammate running on its own virtual machine with a desktop and browser. Users track progress through dedicated threads in the Perplexity app and can interact with the agents via Slack. Perplexity joins SpaceX, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic, which already offer similar agents through Grok Bots, Muse, Dots and Duet. Teammates require the Max plan at $200 per month, while Dots start at $100 and Duet is available from $20, and in practice the cheaper options will likely hit their usage limits fast, days after high agent consumption forced SpaceX to impose stricter usage caps on Grok Bots. Perplexity annualized revenue topped $750 million as of August.
Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Small claims top spot among western open-weight models

Thinking Machines, the startup from former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, is releasing Inkling 2 Small, a mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion parameters of which 17 billion are active at any given time. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 31, an 18 point jump over its predecessor Inkling Small which scored 13, and roughly on par with Google Gemini 3.8 Flash, with especially strong gains in agentic tasks: on AutomationBench-AA the score jumps from 5 to 46 percent and on FrontierCode 2.0 from 5 to 25 percent, and on the knowledge work benchmark AA-Briefcase it hits 1,527 Elo, 615 points above its predecessor. The improved performance comes at a price since the model generates more output tokens and costs six times as much per task as its predecessor. It accepts text and images and offers adjustable thinking depth to choose between speed and thoroughness, and Inkling models are designed as base models for fine-tuning. It is initially available as a proprietary offering through the Tinker platform, with weights under an Apache license to follow.
Anthropic adds Personal Finance so users can connect bank accounts to Claude

Anthropic lets Claude users connect their bank accounts and ask questions about their money through a new feature called Personal Finance, which gives Claude read-only access and cannot move, manage or invest funds. The connection runs through Plaid so Claude never sees a bank password, and users can break down spending by category, check upcoming payments or ask things like whether they are spending more than they earn. The feature launches as a beta in the US for Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers, with Anthropic saying conversations in the Personal Finance section will not be used for model training, that users can disconnect at any time, and that it will not show ads or sponsored recommendations. Longer term Anthropic wants to connect Claude with licensed financial advisors and regulated firms, while OpenAI already offers a similar US feature called Finances.
OpenAI unveils GPT-6 Cyber, a model trained to find, exploit and patch vulnerabilities

OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a model trained specifically to hunt for security vulnerabilities, develop working exploits and suggest patches, and trained to stay within its assigned boundaries. Without any special safety instructions GPT-6 Cyber avoided boundary violations in 99.93 percent of cases, up from 94.49 percent for its predecessor, and with safety instructions enabled it stayed within bounds in 100 percent of tests, with a honeypot inspired by the Hugging Face incident used during training. OpenAI rates GPT-6 Cyber as Critical in the cybersecurity category of its own Preparedness Framework, the same rating given to GPT-6 Astra. On ExploitGym it scores 48.5 percent versus 32.1 percent for predecessor GPT-5.6 Cyber, and on a new test for finding vulnerabilities in web apps without source code access OpenAI reports 40.3 percent versus 32.0 percent for GPT-6 Astra, with GPT-6 Astra with safeguards enabled scoring 0.0 percent. In targeted tests the model found 81 previously unknown critical vulnerabilities in Firefox which Mozilla has already patched, and in the Linux kernel it reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 of them, more than five times as many as its predecessor. All benchmark numbers come from OpenAI itself with no independent testing.
Google Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash goes general availability with 15 second clips and 30 percent lower price

Google DeepMind is making its Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash video generation model generally available. The updated model creates clips up to 15 seconds long, supports conversational editing and costs 30 percent less than its predecessor, rolling out through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Google Cloud Console, Flow, Google Vids, the Gemini app for AI Ultra subscribers and Google Ads. Every generated video carries an imperceptible SynthID watermark, clips now run between three and 15 seconds versus a previous maximum of 10, and pricing drops 30 percent to $0.07 per second for 720p video. Conversational Editing lets users tweak a clip step by step without regenerating, and paired with a tiered workflow where drafts are made at 360p or 720p and only the final result upscaled to 1080p or 4K, it cuts cost. Google also promises better reference adherence and less visual drift or morphing across motion and transitions.
Baidu releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base, a 280B MoE open foundation model without post-training

Baidu released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, an open foundation model that ships deliberately without fine-tuning or post-training, so developers decide where to take it, with a post-trained version supposed to follow. ERNIE 5.5 uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 280 billion parameters of which 14 billion are active per input, was pre-trained on 33.5 trillion tokens with a training context up to 128,000 tokens, and is designed to support context up to one million tokens during fine-tuning and inference. Baidu reports the model competes with similarly sized open foundation models like DeepSeek V4 Flash, Hy3-preview-Base and MiMo V2.5 across exam, STEM, reasoning, knowledge, code, multilingual and long context categories using the same evaluation pipeline. Weights are available on Hugging Face in FP8 and BF16.
The Decoder Frontier Radar #5 profiles 27 neolabs betting against the current AI recipe

OpenAI is talking about the AGI era and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AGI has arrived, with OpenAI president Greg Brockman calling GPT-6 Astra a turning point, while at the same time co-creators of today models are leaving OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Meta to start their own labs, raising billions with no product to show. The Decoder sorted 45 neolabs by research bets, profiled 27 in detail across six bets plus nearly 20 more in brief, and argues the shared motive is doubt about whether today recipe alone, meaning ever-larger language models trained on internet data refined with reinforcement learning, gets to AGI. Named departures include Ilya Sutskever founding Safe Superintelligence, Jerry Tworek running Core Automation, David Silver founding Ineffable Intelligence after AlphaGo, Yann LeCun leaving Meta after twelve years to found AMI, and Jeff Dean after 27 years at Google founding Discovery Loop. The money follows with Nvidia reportedly investing five billion dollars in SSI in July, Prometheus from Jeff Bezos pulling in twelve billion dollars at a 41 billion valuation in June, and Flapping Airplanes raising one billion dollars in an October Series A. The piece notes established companies struggle with ideas that threaten their business, citing the innovator dilemma, with precedents from Transformer at Google in 2017, AlphaGo at DeepMind, and the Anthropic and OpenAI breakouts.
